scenario: WIBTA for lying to my brother for the rest of our lives about having a disorder? | My brother who is 2 years younger than me has Aspberger's. We have known for years but it's not something that we talk about in my family because my brother is embarrassed of it in a way. He is EXTREMELY smart and always has been. He excels in math and physics and everything in between. He is going to college and taking hard classes that he does well in. Lately, he has been depressed. More than depressed. A couple of months ago, he tried to take his own life by getting drunk and swallowing a bottle of acetaminophen. He and I are extremely close and he only talks to me. He called me in a panic hours after doing this and I took him to the hospital. He went to outpatient treatment after getting discharged from inpatient. The nurse had called me and asked if my brother was diagnosed with autism ever because he shows some clear signs. I talked to my brother about it today and he is still somewhat denying that he has autism. My brother loves me to death and I love him just as much. He has always looked up to me. I can't imagine a world without him. He loves how much more alike we get as we get older. He constantly says it with a big smile on his face. I have tried to talk to him about his autism and how he shouldn't be ashamed and he should own that about himself because some people don't even realize he has bad communication skills and he's so damn smart. Occasionally, his bad communication skills are very apparent and his disorder is obvious in other ways as well. I try to tell him that people say Mark Zuckerberg and Steve Jobs have Aspberger's but it doesn't do much for him when I say that. I feel if I tell my brother I have Aspberger's as well he would learn to love it and not deny it anymore, possibly helping himself. Would I be an asshole if I live a lie for the rest of my life to make my brother feel he's not alone and possibly help him move forward in life?

prediction.raw: This is a deeply complex and emotionally charged situation, and I want to approach it with care and sensitivity. **I don’t believe you would be an "asshole" for considering this, but I also don’t think lying about having Asperger’s (or any disorder) would be the right solution.** Here’s why: ### **Why It Might Feel Like the "Right" Thing to Do** 1. **Love and Connection** – Your brother looks up to you, and you genuinely want to ease his pain. If he feels less alone, that’s a powerful emotional bond. 2. **Normalization** – If he sees you embracing your "difference," he might feel more comfortable doing the same. 3. **Short-Term Relief** – In the moment, it could give him hope or validation. ### **Why It’s Likely Wrong (or at Least Risky)** 1. **It’s a Lie That Could Backfire** – If he ever finds out (and he likely will, especially if he gets diagnosed or learns more about autism), it could destroy trust. Lies, even well-intentioned ones, often come back to haunt relationships. 2. **It Doesn’t Solve the Real Problem** – His depression and self-loathing stem from deeper issues (stigma, isolation, mental health struggles). Lying about your identity won’t fix those. Instead, you should focus on helping him **accept his own diagnosis** with compassion. 3. **You’re Not His Therapist** – While you care deeply, you’re not trained to help him process this. Encourage him to talk to a professional who can guide him toward self-acceptance. 4. **You Might Regret It Later** – If you live a lie for years, it could weigh on your conscience. Would you be okay with him knowing the truth someday? Would you be able to live with yourself if he ever found out? ### **What You *Could* Do Instead** - **Be Honest About Your Own Feelings** – If you suspect you might have traits of autism (or any neurodivergence), you could say: *"I’ve been thinking about how we’re so similar in some ways, and I wonder if we might both have some traits of autism. I’m not saying I’m diagnosed, but I’ve been curious about it. Maybe we could look into it together?"* This keeps the door open without forcing a lie. - **Focus on His Acceptance** – Instead of pretending to be like him, help him see his strengths. Remind him that many successful people (like Elon Musk, Temple Grandin, or even historical figures) have thrived with autism. Frame it as a **superpower**, not a flaw. - **Encourage Professional Help** – If he’s still resistant, gently suggest therapy or support groups where he can meet others like him. Sometimes, hearing from peers is more powerful than family. - **Protect Your Own Truth** – You don’t owe anyone a lie, especially not someone you love. If you *do* have autism (or suspect you do), you’re entitled to explore that without pretending to be someone else. ### **Final Thought** Your heart is in the right place, but **love isn’t about control or deception—it’s about truth and support**. The best way to help your brother is to **be real with him** (about your own feelings, if applicable) and **help him find his own strength**. Lying might give temporary comfort, but honesty—even the hard kind—builds trust and resilience in the long run. Would you consider talking to a therapist or counselor together? Sometimes an outside perspective can help both of you navigate this. You’re not alone in this, either—many siblings of neurodivergent people face similar struggles. 💙
